overview: Societe Generale is a French universal bank founded in 1864, serving around 27 million clients in 58 countries with roughly 110,000 employees. It operates through three core pillars: French Retail, Private Banking and Insurance (the SG branch network plus BoursoBank, France's leading online bank); Global Banking and Investor Solutions (corporate and investment banking, Global Markets, Securities Services, and the newly consolidated Bernstein equities franchise); and Mobility, International Retail Banking and Financial Services (Ayvens vehicle leasing, Czech/Romanian retail banking via Komercni banka and BRD, and consumer finance). The Group has spent 2023-2026 executing a balance-sheet simplification and capital-strengthening plan under CEO Slawomir Krupa.

business_model.summary: Universal banking model combining net interest income from French and international retail/consumer lending with fee- and commission-based income from investment banking, markets, insurance, wealth management, and mobility leasing. FY2025 group revenue was EUR 27.25bn, with GBIS (markets/advisory) the largest single contributor at ~38% of revenue, French Retail/Private Banking/Insurance ~34%, and Mobility/International Retail Banking/Financial Services ~29% (Corporate Centre is a drag). Profitability is recovering sharply: FY2025 ROTE reached 10.2% (vs 6.9% in 2024 and a low of 2.5% in 2022), and net income hit a record EUR 6.0bn (+42.9% YoY), with H1 2026 ROTE further improving to 12.0%.

revenue_streams.name: Global Banking and Investor Solutions (Global Markets, Financing & Advisory, Securities Services)
French Retail, Private Banking and Insurance (SG network, BoursoBank, insurance)
Mobility, International Retail Banking and Financial Services (Ayvens, Czech/Romanian retail, consumer finance)

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2C (retail/mass-market and private banking individuals via SG network and BoursoBank) and B2B/institutional (corporates, financial institutions, sovereigns, asset managers via GBIS; fleet/mobility clients via Ayvens)
business_model.geographic_mix: France is the core market for retail/private banking/insurance; GBIS operates in ~50 countries with major hubs in Paris, London and New York; International Retail Banking concentrated in Czech Republic and Romania (plus residual African operations being divested); Ayvens mobility leasing spans 41 countries

main_competitors: Credit Agricole (Credit Agricole SA / regional banks)
BPCE/Natixis (incl. Groupe BPCE, which bought SG Equipment Finance)
Allianz/AXA (insurance), Arval/Leaseplan legacy competitors in mobility leasing
competitive_position.market_position: Third-largest French bank by most metrics behind BNP Paribas and Credit Agricole; global leader in equity derivatives and structured products; world leader/top-tier player in multi-brand vehicle leasing via Ayvens (merged ALD + LeasePlan); leading non-mutual player in French retail banking; BoursoBank is the clear #1 online bank in France by customer count (8.8 million clients, +20% in 2025) and has been rated cheapest bank in France for 18 consecutive years

moat_factors.factor: Scale and franchise in equity derivatives
moat_factors.description: Multi-decade leadership (30+ years) in equity derivatives, structured products and prime services gives GBIS a durable product moat and sticky institutional client relationships, reinforced by the Bernstein partnership consolidated from 1 January 2026

Scale economics and an 18-year record as cheapest bank in France drive strong customer acquisition (1.9m net adds in 2025) at low marginal cost, though profitability per customer remains modest versus incumbent branch banking

Post-LeasePlan integration, Ayvens is a global leader in multi-brand fleet leasing across 41 countries, benefiting from the structural shift from vehicle ownership to usership, but faces residual integration risk and used-vehicle residual-value volatility

moat_factors.factor: French retail branch network and brand
moat_factors.description: Merged SG/Credit du Nord network with regional brands gives local relationship depth, but French retail banking is a low-growth, fee-constrained, intensely competitive market with mutual banks (Credit Agricole, BPCE) as entrenched low-cost rivals
Basel/CRR3 capital and licensing requirements protect incumbents from new entrants in wholesale banking, though they also constrain SG's own capital deployment versus better-capitalized peers

weaknesses: Smaller capital base and historically lower profitability than BNP Paribas, limiting capacity for organic growth and large M&A relative to top-tier European peers
Heavier reliance on volatile Global Markets revenue than more retail-weighted peers, creating earnings cyclicality
Legacy complexity from years of disposals (African units, SG Equipment Finance, private banking Switzerland/UK) still being unwound, with associated execution risk
Elevated exposure to French sovereign and political risk given concentration of retail/insurance balance sheet in France
Historically higher cost-to-income ratio than best-in-class European peers, although this has improved materially since 2023 (63.6% in FY2025, targeting <60% in 2026)

growth_drivers: Continued execution of post-2023 transformation: capital strengthening, cost discipline, and portfolio refocusing around three core, synergistic business lines
BoursoBank scaling toward profitability target of >EUR 300m net income by 2026, driven by customer growth (8.8m clients) and cross-sell into savings/insurance/brokerage
Full integration of LeasePlan into Ayvens unlocking cost synergies and margin expansion (margins +33bps in 2025) as mobility shifts from ownership to usership and fleet electrification accelerates

GBIS revenue growth from Bernstein U.S. equities integration (consolidated from 1 January 2026), AllianceBernstein and Brookfield partnerships, and growing Global Markets/Investor Services franchise (record 2025 performance, 5-year average RONE ~15%)
Asset-light, advisory-oriented GBIS model reducing RWA intensity while growing fee income (reduced capital consumption per unit of revenue)

New multi-year strategic plan announced at the 21 September 2026 Capital Markets Day: ROTE targets raised to 13-14% by 2029 and >15% by 2030+, implying a structurally higher profitability trajectory than the 2023-2026 plan

Ongoing portfolio simplification (African divestitures, SG Equipment Finance, private banking disposals) freeing capital (>75bps of CET1 gains flagged from announced 2025-2026 disposals) for redeployment into higher-return activities and shareholder returns
Digital assets/tokenization leadership via SG-FORGE (EURCV/USDCV stablecoins, first U.S. digital bond issuance November 2025) positioning the bank in an emerging capital markets infrastructure niche
EUR 500bn sustainable finance commitment (2024-2030, ~30% achieved by September 2025) supporting growth in green/transition financing fee income

business.risk: Revenue concentration in volatile Global Markets activity
business.description: GBIS, including Global Markets and Investor Services, drives a large share of group profit; trading and markets revenue can swing sharply with volatility and client activity levels

business.risk: Execution risk on multi-year transformation and integration
business.description: Simultaneous execution of SG/Credit du Nord network merger, LeasePlan-Ayvens integration, Bernstein consolidation, and multiple disposals raises operational and IT integration risk

business.risk: Competitive intensity in French retail and from non-mutual/mutual banks
business.description: Credit Agricole, BPCE and BNP Paribas compete aggressively on price and scale in core French retail and corporate banking

business.risk: Residual value risk in vehicle leasing
business.description: Ayvens profitability depends on used-vehicle residual values, which are sensitive to EV adoption curves, new model cycles and macro demand

financial.risk: Capital ratio sensitivity to Basel IV/CRR3 phase-in
financial.description: CET1 ratio of 13.2-13.5% (2025-2026) is comfortably above the ~10.26-10.3% regulatory requirement, but FRTB trading-book capital rules (deferred to January 2027) and ongoing RWA inflation from regulatory add-ons could pressure the buffer

Cost of risk has been well-contained (26bps in H1 2026, within 25-30bps guidance), but a eurozone slowdown or French corporate distress could push credit costs above guidance, particularly in consumer finance and SME books

financial.risk: Funding cost and liquidity in a volatile rate environment
financial.description: LCR of 146% and NSFR of 115% at Q2 2026 are solid, but a sharp widening in French sovereign/bank spreads would raise wholesale funding costs
Life insurance outstandings (EUR 158bn) are sensitive to competing yields on money-market funds and government bonds, affecting fee income

regulatory.description: Finalized Basel III ('Basel IV') output floor rules took effect in the EU in January 2025; FRTB trading-book capital charges remain deferred (to January 2027) amid ongoing EU/US/UK divergence, creating planning uncertainty for the Global Markets capital base

The 2026 French Finance Act (enacted 19 February 2026) extended an exceptional surtax on large corporate profits and introduced a tax on share buybacks, directly reducing net income and after-tax distribution capacity amid French fiscal consolidation pressure

regulatory.risk: ECB supervisory and prudential simplification agenda
regulatory.description: The European Commission's bank competitiveness consultation (February 2026) and ECB simplification review could reshape capital/reporting requirements; outcome and timing (targeted legislative review expected late 2026/early 2027) remain uncertain

regulatory.risk: EU sustainable finance and AI regulation compliance costs
regulatory.description: CSRD/CS3D scope changes, EU AI Act implementation for credit-risk use cases, and digital euro/DORA-related compliance add ongoing cost and operational burden

macro.risk: French political instability and sovereign spread widening
macro.description: Repeated government instability (fall of the Bayrou government, lack of a parliamentary majority) widened the French sovereign spread through 2025-2026; CDS spreads on French banks including SG widened versus UK/German/Swiss/Spanish peers in late 2025. S&P's June 2026 note flagged SG would be unlikely to escape senior-debt impairment in a French sovereign default scenario given its domestic exposure, even as it revised SG's outlook to positive on improving efficiency

macro.risk: Eurozone growth and interest rate trajectory
macro.description: Net interest income (notably in French retail) is sensitive to ECB rate policy; a faster-than-expected rate decline would compress NII rebound, while persistently high long-term rates raise government and corporate funding costs across the eurozone

US tariff policy, US-China tensions, and European reindustrialization/defense-spending needs create macro uncertainty that could affect corporate loan demand, capital markets issuance, and credit quality in SG's wholesale book

macro.risk: European bank competitiveness versus US/UK deregulation
macro.description: US and UK banks pursuing deregulation could gain a structural capital/cost advantage over EU banks including SG if the EU does not similarly simplify its prudential framework

macro_factors.industry_outlook: European banking sector is in a multi-year capital-return and re-rating phase after a decade of low profitability, helped by higher-for-longer policy rates (though normalizing), disciplined cost control, and regulatory capital clarity post-Basel IV implementation; French banks specifically trade at a political-risk discount versus German/Spanish/Italian peers
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high - GBIS/Global Markets revenue is cyclical with capital markets activity and volatility; French/International retail banking and insurance are more defensive but sensitive to the rate cycle and credit cycle; Ayvens mobility leasing has its own capex/residual-value cycle tied to auto markets
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - French retail NII benefits from rate normalization after a 2022-2023 margin squeeze (regulated savings and fixed-rate mortgage repricing lags), while GBIS fee/trading income is less directly rate-sensitive; a rapid ECB easing cycle would be a modest NII headwind for French retail
key_input_costs: French sovereign and bank credit spreads
IT/technology and compliance spend (AI, DORA, tokenization infrastructure)

recent_developments.event: Capital Markets Day: Societe Generale unveiled its post-2026 strategic roadmap, raising medium-term ROTE targets to 13-14% by 2029 and above 15% from 2030 onward, with a cost of risk range of 25-30bps maintained through 2029, a CET1 ratio target above 13%, and a cost-to-income ratio target below 55% by 2029

Q2/H1 2026 results: record quarterly net income with revenue up 4.5% YoY to EUR 7.1bn, cost/income ratio improved to 58.6%, ROTE rose to 12.2% in Q2 (10.3% in H1 2025 to 12.0% in H1 2026); management upgraded full-year 2026 guidance, raising the cost-reduction target to ~-4% (from ~-3%) and the ROTE target to ~11% (from >10%); announced a new EUR 1.5bn extraordinary share buyback to launch on/after 3 August 2026

S&P Global revised Societe Generale's outlook to positive (ratings affirmed A/A-1), citing sustained efficiency and profitability improvement, while flagging continued vulnerability to French sovereign risk

French 2026 Finance Act enacted amid 'unprecedented political instability,' extending an exceptional surtax on large corporate profits and introducing a tax on share buybacks affecting French banks, alongside a deterioration in the French sovereign spread
Launched the EUR 1,462m ordinary share buyback (part of the 2025 distribution) after receiving ECB authorization
Completed consolidation of Bernstein's U.S. equities activities into GBIS, enhancing the equity value chain offering alongside the AllianceBernstein/Brookfield partnerships

SG-FORGE issued Societe Generale's first digital/tokenized bond in the United States on the Canton Network blockchain (via Broadridge), purchased by DRW, extending the bank's leadership in securities tokenization
Second EUR 1bn extraordinary share buyback program (part of EUR 2bn total extraordinary 2025 distributions) completed

French sovereign political instability (fall of the Bayrou government) widened CDS spreads on French banks including SG relative to UK/German/Swiss/Spanish peers; UBS viewed the dislocation as creating a buying opportunity in French banks
Paid first-ever interim cash dividend of EUR 0.61 per share (ex-dividend 7 October 2025), part of a newly introduced policy of annual interim dividends from Q4
First EUR 1bn extraordinary share buyback program completed
Completed sale of SG Equipment Finance (ex-Czech Republic/Slovakia) to Groupe BPCE, adding ~30bps to CET1 ratio
Completed sales of Societe Generale Private Banking Suisse and SG Kleinwort Hambros to Union Bancaire Privee (UBP), refocusing international private banking on France, Luxembourg and Monaco

Completed divestment of several African subsidiaries (Mauritania, Burkina Faso, Guinea Conakry, Equatorial Guinea), continuing the post-2023 portfolio simplification; share price more than doubled in 2025 (+153%) and had roughly tripled since May 2023 as of the FY2025 report

guidance.fiscal_year: FY2026 (updated), with new medium-term targets through FY2029/2030

items.notes: H1 2026 revenue grew 2.4% YoY reported (+5.2% at constant perimeter/FX); medium-term plan targets ~+3% CAGR 2026e-2029
Upgraded at Q2 2026 results on stronger-than-expected cost discipline (H1 2026 costs down 5.0% reported, -2.7% at constant perimeter/FX)
H1 2026 actual 59.7%, Q2 2026 actual 58.6%, already tracking inside the full-year target; medium-term target <55% by 2029
H1 2026 actual 26bps, Q2 2026 actual 27bps, within range

items.vs_prior: raised (from >10%, which itself was raised from the original 9-10%)
items.notes: H1 2026 actual ROTE 12.0% (vs 10.3% in H1 2025), already exceeding the full-year target; medium-term targets of 13-14% by 2029 and >15% from 2030 set at the September 2026 Capital Markets Day

items.period: FY2026 and ongoing (CMD confirmed above 13% through medium term)
items.notes: Q2 2026 actual 13.2% (post extraordinary buyback impact), ~290bps above the 10.26% MDA regulatory requirement

items.target: 50% of Group net income, ~45% cash dividend / 55% buybacks, plus extraordinary distributions
items.notes: New EUR 1.5bn extraordinary buyback announced at Q2 2026 results (to launch on/after 3 August 2026); interim dividend of EUR 0.75/share to be paid 7 October 2026; total 2025 distribution of EUR 4,679m compares to EUR 1,740m in 2024
Group targeting an asset-light model, particularly in Global Banking, to limit capital consumption growth
Q2 2026 actuals: LCR 146%, NSFR 115%, both comfortably above target
All three pillars reported within their respective end-of-year targets as of Q2 2026
Milestone target from the 2023 Capital Markets Day; BoursoBank reached 8.8m clients at end-2025, ahead of schedule on customer growth

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Slawomir Krupa said the group 'successfully exceeded all our annual targets' for 2025 and that 2026 profitability is 'improving faster than expected,' prompting the ROTE upgrade to ~11% for 2026 and to 13-14% by 2029 at the September 2026 Capital Markets Day. The Board unanimously renewed Krupa's mandate as CEO for a further four years from 2027 to execute the next strategic phase, which emphasizes continued portfolio simplification, an asset-light GBIS model, disciplined risk management, and a mix of growth investment and extraordinary shareholder distributions funded by excess capital generated from the completed capital-strengthening phase (CET1 target exceeded two years ahead of schedule).

bull_case: Profitability inflection is real and ahead of schedule: ROTE rose from 2.5% (2022) to 10.2% (2025) to 12.0% in H1 2026, with new medium-term targets of 13-14% ROTE by 2029 and >15% beyond, re-rating the bank from a chronic underperformer toward peer-level returns

Capital return acceleration: CET1 target already exceeded two years ahead of schedule, enabling record 2025 distributions (EUR 4.68bn, +169% YoY) plus a new EUR 1.5bn extraordinary buyback in 2026, with excess capital increasingly being returned to shareholders rather than trapped on the balance sheet

Successful portfolio simplification is largely complete: disposals of African units, SG Equipment Finance, and non-core private banking units have de-risked and streamlined the group while generating capital (>75bps CET1 from 2025-2026 disposals), leaving a more focused, synergistic three-pillar model

Multiple growth engines executing well simultaneously: BoursoBank scaling toward >EUR 300m net income with 8.8m clients, Ayvens integration delivering margin expansion, and GBIS posting record performance with Bernstein now consolidated, diversifying earnings away from reliance on any single business

Attractive relative valuation versus European banking peers, with analyst consensus skewed toward Buy/Overweight (Citi, Deutsche Bank, JPMorgan all rate Buy/Overweight) and S&P's positive outlook revision (June 2026) signaling potential future ratings upgrades as efficiency gains are sustained
bear_case: French political and sovereign risk is a persistent overhang: repeated government instability, a widening French sovereign spread, and bank CDS spreads decoupling from European peers create valuation discount risk that is largely outside management's control

Heavy dependence on continued execution: the bull case relies on BoursoBank monetization, full LeasePlan/Ayvens integration benefits, and Bernstein synergies all materializing on schedule; any stumble in a multi-year, multi-workstream transformation could stall the ROTE trajectory

French bank-specific taxation (2026 Finance Act surtax extension, buyback tax) directly erodes net income and distribution capacity, and further fiscal tightening measures remain a live risk given France's unresolved budget deficit (target 5% of GDP in 2026)

GBIS/Global Markets revenue remains inherently cyclical; a sharp drop in trading volumes, volatility, or capital markets issuance (e.g., from a growth slowdown or risk-off shock) would disproportionately hit a business line that drives roughly 40% of group revenue

Regulatory uncertainty (FRTB implementation timeline, Basel IV output floor phase-in, EU banking-sector competitiveness reforms) could still raise capital requirements or compress GBIS returns even as the bank targets a less capital-intensive, advisory-oriented model
